power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p < .05", Text = "Lines indicate significant partial correlations (p < .05)."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = .301", "p = .179 "), Sentence = c("This model increased parsimony without significantly worsening model fit, Δ χ 2 (5) = 6.06, p = .301, and had good model fit χ 2 (130) = 182.35, CFI = 0.95, RMSEA = 0.05, 90% CI [0.03, 0.06], SRMR = 0.06.", "This modification increased parsimony without significantly worsening model fit, Δ χ 2 (1) = 1.80, p = .179 The resulting model had good fit, χ 2 ( 131 N ." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

info.title: Binding Memory and Relational Mechanisms: The Central Role of Binding in Fluid Intelligence

text.text: Fluid intelligence (Gf) and working memory (WM) are strongly correlated, with the binding hypothesis suggesting that this relationship is driven by the capacity to bind content to context.
However, it remains unclear how various binding functions overlap and relate to Gf.

This study investigates the extent of overlap between five binding functions (item-tolocation binding, item-to-item binding, relational integration, relation processing, and perceptual feature binding) and their relationship with Gf.
A sample of 174 young adults completed three visuospatial variants of tasks measuring these five binding functions alongside three Gf tasks.
Data were analyzed using structural equation modeling and latent network analysis to evaluate shared and unique variances.
Results indicated significant overlap among the binding functions, with item-to-location and item-to-item binding best modeled as a single latent variable termed binding memory.

The shared variance among binding memory and the remaining binding functions was represented by a higher-order, process-general latent factor labeled Binding which was found to be statistically isomorphic with Gf.

Latent network analysis further revealed that binding memory, relational integration, and relation processing each exhibited unique, direct relationships with Gf, whereas perceptual feature binding related to Gf only indirectly.

These findings indicate that an overarching, domain-general ability to form and utilize bindings in a goal-directed manner is deeply intertwined with Gf, supporting theories emphasizing binding and relational mechanisms in Gf.

A central goal in cognitive psychology is to understand the mechanisms that underlie fluid intelligence (Gf) and working memory (WM), because both Gf and WM support understanding and interacting with the environment, enabling crucial daily activities, such as cooking, reading, and navigating.
Gf is the ability to reason and solve new problems, and WM is the ability to maintain and manipulate information for ongoing processing.
Gf is strongly related to WM capacity (WMC; Kyllonen & Christal, 1990), but it is not clear why.
text.formatted: Gf is strongly related to WM capacity (WMC; <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Kyllonen & Christal, 1990</ref>), but it is not clear why.

text.text: Understanding the relationship between Gf and WMC is crucial for building comprehensive models and theories of cognition.

One explanation for the WMC-Gf relationship is the binding hypothesis, which proposes that WMC and Gf are predominantly limited by the capacity for bindings between content and context representations rather than individual representations in WM (Oberauer, 2009; Oberauer et al., 2007).
text.formatted: One explanation for the WMC-Gf relationship is the binding hypothesis, which proposes that WMC and Gf are predominantly limited by the capacity for bindings between content and context representations rather than individual representations in WM <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Oberauer, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Oberauer et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Whereas individual representations convey information about single elements (e.g., a cat), binding representations can convey relational information (e.g., a cat chasing a dog).
The binding hypothesis specifies that such relational information is necessary for Gf.

Specifically, the comparison and application of relational information are proposed to be necessary for inductive (Klauer, 1996) and deductive (Goodwin & Johnson-Laird, 2005) reasoning such that greater capacity for relational information allows for more complex reasoning.
text.formatted: Specifically, the comparison and application of relational information are proposed to be necessary for inductive <ref type="bibr">(Klauer, 1996)</ref> and deductive <ref type="bibr">(Goodwin & Johnson-Laird, 2005)</ref> reasoning such that greater capacity for relational information allows for more complex reasoning.

text.text: Thus, the binding hypothesis suggests that greater WMC equates to greater binding capacity, which allows for the comparison and application of more relational information and, thus, higher Gf (Oberauer et al., 2007 (Oberauer et al., , 2008)).
text.formatted: Thus, the binding hypothesis suggests that greater WMC equates to greater binding capacity, which allows for the comparison and application of more relational information and, thus, higher Gf <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Oberauer et al., 2007</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Oberauer et al., , 2008))</ref>.

text.text: The binding hypothesis is mostly supported by evidence showing that binding errors, in which content in WM is bound to the incorrect context, occur more often than item errors, in which representations are recalled that are not bound to any task-relevant context (Bartsch & Oberauer, 2023; Henson et al., 1996; Oberauer, 2019; Pertzov et al., 2012).
text.formatted: The binding hypothesis is mostly supported by evidence showing that binding errors, in which content in WM is bound to the incorrect context, occur more often than item errors, in which representations are recalled that are not bound to any task-relevant context <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bartsch & Oberauer, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Henson et al., 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Oberauer, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Pertzov et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: For example, Henson and colleagues (Henson et al., 1996) investigated recall for letters bound to their serial position and found that item errors only accounted for 3% of the total errors while binding errors accounted for 92% of all errors. Bartsch and Oberauer (2023) found a similar difference in the frequency of binding and item errors when using pictures bound to words and additionally found that item memory was unaffected by set size.

text.text: However, critical questions about the relation between binding, WMC, and Gf remain.
First, it is possible that other abilities pertaining to binding, not binding capacity, are associated with Gf.

For example, Chuderski (2019) examined the association between Gf and relation processing (the ability to represent, transform, and apply relations in the mind), operationalized with a relation matching task.
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Chuderski (2019)</ref> examined the association between Gf and relation processing (the ability to represent, transform, and apply relations in the mind), operationalized with a relation matching task.

text.text: In this task participants need to match identical bindings that stay on screen (for details and an illustration of our adaptation, see Method).
Therefore, this task requires binding but is assumed to have minimal requirements on WMC.
Nevertheless, strong associations with Gf were observed, suggesting that individual differences in Gf may be driven by binding but not binding capacity.

Second, (Oberauer et al., 2007) proposed that the capacity for binding is limited by binding interference which occurs as a result of retrieval competition and representational interference between overlapping bindings.
text.formatted: Second, <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Oberauer et al., 2007)</ref> proposed that the capacity for binding is limited by binding interference which occurs as a result of retrieval competition and representational interference between overlapping bindings.

text.text: However, recent research found a lack of individual differences specific to the ability to manage binding interference (Garvey et al., 2026), questioning the viability of binding interference as the driver of individual differences in binding capacity and, therefore, WMC and Gf.
text.formatted: However, recent research found a lack of individual differences specific to the ability to manage binding interference <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Garvey et al., 2026)</ref>, questioning the viability of binding interference as the driver of individual differences in binding capacity and, therefore, WMC and Gf.

text.text: Along with relation processing, several binding functions have been proposed that have conceptual and, possibly, mechanistic overlap, and it is unclear how these abilities are related to each other and to Gf: item-to-location binding, item-to-item binding, relational integration, relation processing, and perceptual feature binding.
The purpose of this study is to determine the extent of the overlap between these binding functions and their relationship with Gf.
While binding capacity is thought to reflect a general ability, distinct types of binding may utilize different cognitive mechanisms.
For example, an item can be bound to the space it had occupied (item-to-location) or to another item representation (item-to-item).

Item-tolocation binding is operationalized with the local recognition task in which participants are sequentially shown items in different locations and then indicate whether probes represent the same items in the same locations (Oberauer, 2003).
text.formatted: Item-tolocation binding is operationalized with the local recognition task in which participants are sequentially shown items in different locations and then indicate whether probes represent the same items in the same locations <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Oberauer, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Item-to-item binding is operationalized with the associated-pairs task in which participants are sequentially shown pairs of items and then indicate whether probes represent the same pairs that were previously shown (e.g., Wilhelm et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Item-to-item binding is operationalized with the associated-pairs task in which participants are sequentially shown pairs of items and then indicate whether probes represent the same pairs that were previously shown (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Wilhelm et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Shared variance in performance on the local recognition task (item-to-location binding) and the associated-pairs task (item-to-item binding) has been used in past research to indicate binding ability (De Simoni & von Bastian, 2018; Garvey et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Shared variance in performance on the local recognition task (item-to-location binding) and the associated-pairs task (item-to-item binding) has been used in past research to indicate binding ability <ref type="bibr">(De Simoni & von Bastian, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Garvey et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: However, because it involves representations of two items, itemto-item binding may provide greater semantic richness than item-to-location binding.
Semantic richness may facilitate retrieval from long-term memory (Brady et al., 2013; Konkle et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Semantic richness may facilitate retrieval from long-term memory <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Brady et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Konkle et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: This difference in the utilization of long-term memory may affect the variance that is shared between item-to-item and item-to-location binding.
For example, representations in long-term memory may be less susceptible to binding interference.

Indeed, it may be that Garvey et al. (2026) was unable to find significant individual differences in the ability to manage binding interference because this ability was indicated by shared variance in local recognition and associated-pairs tasks.
text.formatted: Indeed, it may be that <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Garvey et al. (2026)</ref> was unable to find significant individual differences in the ability to manage binding interference because this ability was indicated by shared variance in local recognition and associated-pairs tasks.

text.text: If the associated-pairs task utilizes long-term memory, and long-term memory is not susceptible to binding interference, then the shared variance between the associated-pairs and local recognition tasks would not be indicative of binding interference.
Another proposed binding function is relational integration, which is the ability to integrate bindings into structural representations.

In context of the binding hypothesis, structural representations permit the comparison and application of relational information and, therefore, reasoning ability (Oberauer, 2009; Oberauer et al., 2008).
text.formatted: In context of the binding hypothesis, structural representations permit the comparison and application of relational information and, therefore, reasoning ability <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Oberauer, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Oberauer et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Relational integration has been found to positively relate to Gf even when statistically accounting for differences in mental speed and storage factors (Krumm et al., 2009).
text.formatted: Relational integration has been found to positively relate to Gf even when statistically accounting for differences in mental speed and storage factors <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Krumm et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, relational integration predicted Gf better than other cognitive abilities, namely attention control and short-term memory (Chuderski, 2014), and performance on complex span tasks (Chuderski, 2014; Oberauer et al., 2008).
text.formatted: Furthermore, relational integration predicted Gf better than other cognitive abilities, namely attention control and short-term memory <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Chuderski, 2014)</ref>, and performance on complex span tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Chuderski, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Oberauer et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Recently, relation processing has been shown to be strongly related to Gf; it only requires the ability to match relations between bindings rather than building structural representations via relational integration (Chuderski, 2019).
text.formatted: Recently, relation processing has been shown to be strongly related to Gf; it only requires the ability to match relations between bindings rather than building structural representations via relational integration <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Chuderski, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: While relation processing would appear to be necessary for relational integration -assuming that relations need to be processed before they are integrated -the relationship between relational integration and relation processing has not been investigated.
It may be that the relationship between relational integration and Gf found in previous studies is at least partially attributable to relation processing.
Moreover, the relation between Gf and binding may be due to a lower-level cognitive process than relation processing -one that does not require WM.
For example, perceptual feature binding is the ability to bind simultaneously presented features into a single coherent object before or during WM encoding.
Perceptual feature binding has been studied for decades (Kovacs & Harris, 2019; Treisman & Gelade, 1980; Wolfe & Cave, 1999), using a wide variety of tasks.
text.formatted: Perceptual feature binding has been studied for decades <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Kovacs & Harris, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Treisman & Gelade, 1980;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Wolfe & Cave, 1999)</ref>, using a wide variety of tasks.

text.text: Traditionally, these tasks would present objects outside the spatial attentional spotlight, and examine whether a target's low-level features (e.g., color, orientation) are correctly bound together or incorrectly fused with a nearby distractor.
Here, we used a variant of the rapid serial visual presentation (RSVP) task, where participants are shown images sequentially in the same location at a rate of 100 ms per item.
Participants are asked to report a target item that is cued, for example, by a frame.
In this task, binding errors occur frequently.

Specifically, the item appearing immediately after the cued item is often erroneously reported as the target (Botella et al., 2001; Chun, 1997; Zivony & Eimer, 2023), indicating perceptual feature binding across time.
text.formatted: Specifically, the item appearing immediately after the cued item is often erroneously reported as the target <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Botella et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Chun, 1997;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Zivony & Eimer, 2023)</ref>, indicating perceptual feature binding across time.

text.text: Individual differences in this kind of feature binding have not been the topic of much investigation, but a recent study showed that these perceptual binding errors are highly reliable and stable over time (Zivony et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Individual differences in this kind of feature binding have not been the topic of much investigation, but a recent study showed that these perceptual binding errors are highly reliable and stable over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Zivony et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The inclusion of the RSVP task allowed us to examine whether Gf is predicted uniquely by WM binding, or by binding at a lower cognitive level.

The goal of this study was to determine the extent to which five binding functionsitem-to-location binding, item-to-item binding, relational integration, relation processing, and perceptual feature binding -overlap and relate to Gf.
We compared latent variable models beginning with a model which has six correlated latent variables representing each function and Gf.
We systematically modified each model by reducing the number of latent variables until further reductions did not improve model fit.
We also used latent network analysis to model the partial correlations between latent variables to reveal any binding functions that have unique relationships with Gf.
We expected to find that each function significantly relates to each other and to Gf, but we had no prediction for the magnitude of their overlap.

text.text: A total of 201 young adults were recruited from Sheffield, England through Sona Systems, posters, social media advertisements, and word of mouth.

To determine the extent of the overlap between binding functions, we used a stepwise model comparison approach beginning with the baseline structural equation model (excluding Gf) where indicators loaded onto their respective paradigm-specific latent factors.
In each subsequent step, we identified the two latent factors with the strongest correlation and tested a nested model in which these factors merged into a single factor.
If merging the factors did not significantly worsen model fit compared to the baseline model, we retained the nested model as the reference model and compared subsequent models to this model.

If the fit significantly worsened, we tested a nested model that merged the pair of factors with the next-highest correlation, comparing it with the baseline model or the reference model if one was established.
This process continued until no further factors could be combined without significant loss of fit.
We also explored a model (excluding Gf) in which each paradigm-specific latent factor loaded onto a higher-order latent factor.
Latent network analysis was performed on the best-fitting model to explore the unique relationships between binding functions and Gf.
In a latent-network model, network nodes represent latent variables, and edges represent the conditional dependent associations (also known as partial correlations) between pairs of connected nodes.
All network models are estimated by modeling the variance-covariance matrix of the data in Gaussian graphical models (Epskamp et al., 2018).

This study investigated relations among binding functions (item-to-location binding, item-to-item binding, relational integration, relation processing, and perceptual feature binding) and between binding and Gf.
All binding functions correlated strongly with Gf, though perceptual feature binding showed the weakest correlations with other binding functions as well as with Gf.

Complementing these findings, network analysis revealed that binding memory, relation processing, and relational integration but not perceptual feature binding were uniquely related to Gf, setting perceptual feature binding somewhat apart from the other binding functions.
Furthermore, only item-to-location binding and item-to-item binding could be represented by a single combined latent variable -binding memory.
Binding memory and the other binding functions shared a high amount of variance which could be represented without significant loss of fit by a higher-order ability -Binding.
Statistically, Binding was isomorphic with Gf indicating that individual differences in one ability are highly similar to individual differences in the other.

Binding memory represents all that the local recognition and associated-pairs tasks have in common, which includes, but is not limited to, the ability to store, maintain, and retrieve content-context bindings in WM as well as familiarity-based retrieval (see Limitations).
Moreover, given previous evidence suggesting that WMC is limited by binding capacity (for reviews, see Oberauer, 2009; Oberauer et al., 2007), we cannot conclude that binding memory is WMC.

text.text: Indeed, this possibility may be reflected in the network analysis results, which showed that binding memory had the strongest unique association with Gf among all binding functions; this pattern may reflect the well-established strong relationship between WMC and Gf (Engle et al., 1999; Kyllonen & Christal, 1990).

text.text: Although item-to-item and item-to-location binding appear to differ in the semantic richness of their binding contexts -a factor evidenced to facilitate retrieval from long-term memory (Brady et al., 2013; Konkle et al., 2010) -they were best represented by a single variable: binding memory.

text.text: If there were a substantial mechanistic difference in item-to-item and item-to-location binding regarding semantic processing, this would be reflected as distinct variables of item-to-location and item-to-item in our models.

Instead, our models favor a single latent variable of item-to-item and item-to-location binding, suggesting little inherent difference in semantic processing between item-to-location and item-to-item binding.
This result is consistent with Konkle et al. (2010), whose findings suggest that scene and object categories are represented at a similar level of abstraction in long-term memory.
text.formatted: This result is consistent with <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Konkle et al. (2010)</ref>, whose findings suggest that scene and object categories are represented at a similar level of abstraction in long-term memory.

text.text: To the extent that item-to-item bindings could be considered simple scenes in general, then in comparison to objects (item-to-location bindings), they have similar levels of abstraction in long-term memory.

Therefore, item-to-item and item-to-location binding may not differ in retrieval from long-term memory, which was the potential mechanism through which semantic richness differentiated item-to-item and item-to-location binding.
Relation processing exhibited remarkably strong relationships with Gf, other binding functions, and the process-general Binding factor.
Supporting the findings from Chuderski (2019), relation processing was identifiable as a latent factor across tasks using diverse visual and spatial stimuli and was highly correlated with Gf.

text.text: Thus, Chuderski's (2019) conclusion that single simple bindings are critical for Gf is supported by the current study.

text.text: Moreover, relation processing directly related to Gf in the network analysis, indicating that their relationship is not entirely accounted for by relational integration or other binding functions (although their direct relationship was smaller, ranging from r = .78 to rxy.z = .32).
Similar to relation processing, relational integration was highly related to Gf, the other binding functions, and the overarching latent Binding factor.

Network analysis revealed unique relationships between relational integration, relation processing, and Gf, indicating that although relation processing and integration are highly related, the shared variance between relational integration and Gf is not entirely accounted for by relation processing or the other binding functions.
This finding is consistent with previous studies that found strong relationships between relational integration and Gf (Chuderski, 2014; Krumm et al., 2009; Oberauer et al., 2008).
text.formatted: This finding is consistent with previous studies that found strong relationships between relational integration and Gf <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Chuderski, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Krumm et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Oberauer et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: However, because of their strong interrelationship, relational integration and relation processing are difficult to disentangle and might have been confounded in previous studies.
The present results make this interrelation explicit and show that relational integration and Gf are associated above and beyond of what they share with relation processing, and vice versa.
Perceptual feature binding shared significant variance with the other binding functions, suggesting that it draws partly on common mechanisms.

At the same time, it loaded less strongly on Binding and was not directly connected to Gf in the network; rather, its association with Gf was accounted for by its shared variance with relation processing and integration.

Together, these findings suggest that perceptual and WM binding are neither fully separable nor equivalent: perceptual binding relies substantially on processes specific to perception, yet it is embedded in the broader binding system that supports reasoning.
Notably, the RSVP task used to assess perceptual feature binding involved no retention interval, making it unlikely that the shared variance reflects WM maintenance demands.

Instead, the overlap may arise at the stage at which perceptually bound features are selected and consolidated into WM (see also (Ricker et al., 2018), suggesting that perception and WM interact closely during the formation of bindings.

text.text: The latent network analysis revealed differences in the pathways connecting the binding functions to each other and to Gf.
Although the binding functions were all highly correlated, Gf accounted for most of the relationship between binding memory and both relational integration and relation processing.

To some extent, this pattern of results may be reflective of the domain-generality of Gf and, by extension, Binding; binding functions may have been related only indirectly because they are representative of different process domains.
If the binding functions tap into distinct process domains, only an overarching, process-general mechanism, like Gf, could capture variance shared between these functions.

The groupings of the binding functions in the network analysis may suggest three process domains: binding memory, relational mechanisms (relational integration and relation processing), and perceptual feature binding.
Mechanistic differences between these process domains are apparent in the representational demands.

Relational mechanisms require processing multidimensional relations between representations (i.e., the direction of the slash as well as the items in the relational representation task, and the direction of the match across the grid in the monitoring task), and these relations must be processed for goalattainment.
In contrast, for binding memory, the relationship between items or between an item and a location is binary: the content is either bound to the probed context or it is not.
Finally, perceptual feature binding differs from binding memory and relational mechanisms in that it is binding at the perceptual rather than WM level.

However, perceptual feature binding is directly related to relational mechanisms -possibly indicative of the theoretical expectation that perceptual feature binding serves as a foundational prerequisite for complex relational mechanisms.
These differences in representational demands among binding memory, relational mechanisms, and perceptual feature binding may underpin their different relations to Gf.

Another possibility is that the distinction between binding memory and relational mechanisms reflect differing demands on attention control and that Gf is representative of individual differences in attention control.
Attention control is defined as the ability to direct attention and ignore internal and external distractors in pursuit of a goal (Engle, 2002).
text.formatted: Attention control is defined as the ability to direct attention and ignore internal and external distractors in pursuit of a goal <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Engle, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: The disengagement hypothesis proposes that attention control supports the maintenance of representations in WM and the disengagement from irrelevant information and false hypotheses to the benefit of Gf (Burgoyne et al., 2022; Shipstead & Engle, 2013).
text.formatted: The disengagement hypothesis proposes that attention control supports the maintenance of representations in WM and the disengagement from irrelevant information and false hypotheses to the benefit of Gf <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Burgoyne et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Shipstead & Engle, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Indeed, the current findings map onto the mechanisms of the disengagement hypothesis.

Specifically, binding memory aligns with the maintenance of representations in WM, while relational integration, relation processing, and perceptual feature binding could all require inhibiting irrelevant information and, thus, disengagement.
As such, Gf may have accounted for much of the relationship between binding memory and the other binding functions because it represents shared variance in attention control.

However, the measurement of attention control remains debated; many studies find weak correlations between measures of attention control (Keye et al., 2009; Rey-Mermet et al., 2019; Shilling et al., 2002; von Bastian et al., 2020).

text.text: Moreover, when influences of processing speed are accounted for, measures of attention control do not significantly correlate with WMC or Gf (Rey-Mermet et al., 2019).

text.text: The attention control account of the current results should, therefore, be interpreted with caution.

The common thread across the tasks used in this study to assess the five binding functions is the ability to form and make use of bindings in a goal-directed manner, so this is likely what the second-order factor Binding represents.

The overlap between Binding and Gf supports theories of Gf or complex reasoning in which Gf depends on bindings, such as the binding hypothesis (Oberauer, 2009) or the relation processing account (Chuderski, 2022).

text.text: Importantly, binding memory, relation processing, and relational integration each correlated with Gf independently of each other -indicating that none of these specific binding functions could completely account for individual differences in Gf.
Rather, the more process-general Binding factor was isomorphic with Gf, which is consistent with previous findings that highlight the association of binding maintenance with Gf (Garvey et al. 2026).

text.text: By demonstrating that a process-general Binding can explain nearly all reliable variance in Gf, the current results suggest that binding constitutes an even more central constraint on Gf than these previous, domain-specific studies could reveal.
A strength of this study was the use of the same sets of visual/spatial stimuli for each binding paradigm.

Using the same stimuli sets allowed us to focus the shared variance on paradigm-specific mechanisms (the binding functions) and pre-emptively remove error variance due to stimulus-specific variance that might have otherwise varied between paradigms.
Furthermore, each stimulus set was chosen to differ meaningfully from each other to mitigate the influence of specific task strategies (e.g., verbal labelling).
The fractals were meaningless, colorful, and visually complex.
The arrows were more meaningful, blackand-white, and less complex than the fractals but were identical to each other apart from orientation and thickness.
The symbols were the most meaningful, black-and-white, and less visually similar than the arrows.
These considerations likely contributed to the strong correlations, high factor loadings, and good model fits observed in the structural equation models.
However, using the same sets of stimuli for each paradigm and using only visual/spatial Gf tasks could also be considered a limitation.
It is possible that shared method variance artificially inflated factor loadings and the correlations between the latent factors.
Additionally, because we only used visual/spatial tasks, we cannot definitively conclude that the present results extend to verbal/numerical domains.

While some research suggests that WMC is largely domain-general (e.g., Vergauwe et al., 2022), future research should use a broader array of stimulus domains to investigate the domain-general nature of the Binding-Gf isomorphism.

text.text: One limitation of the current study is the influence of individual differences in response criterion.

As in past research (De Simoni & von Bastian, 2018a; Prieto et al., 2023; Talmi & Goshen-Gottstein, 2006; Thompson et al., 2013; von Bastian et al., 2013; von Bastian & Eschen, 2016), we used the discrimination parameter d' to isolate recollection from familiarity-based performance in the local recognition and associated-pairs tasks.

Future research should implement methods for gauging individual difference in participants' response criterion, such as receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves of participants' confidence ratings (see Brady et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Future research should implement methods for gauging individual difference in participants' response criterion, such as receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves of participants' confidence ratings (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Brady et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Individual differences in evidence weighting may have contributed to another caveat of the current results: that the split-half reliability estimates were low for the associated pairs and local recognition tasks, especially for the fractals associated-pairs task.
The fractals associated-pairs task may have had particularly low reliability due to differences in the distinctiveness between the fractal stimuli.
Participants may have benefited from labeling the shapes and colors for certain fractal pairs but not others.
For example, only one fractal was black and white, while multiple fractals were red.
Labeling the black and white fractal may have facilitated recognition, but labeling the red fractals may have resulted in more false alarms.

Regardless, the latent variables of local recognition, associated pairs, and binding memory were identifiable with high loading coefficients, indicating that the individual local recognition and associated-pairs tasks measured the same variable to some extent.

Given the importance of understanding the mechanisms that underlie Gf, and the current findings that show substantial overlap between Gf and process-general Binding, future research should investigate additional binding functions that could be encompassed by Binding.

The present study only targeted extrinsic bindings (the relations between items and independent spatiotemporal contexts or other items), but intrinsic bindings (the integration of features of a single, unified item; i.e., working memory feature binding) may exhibit different patterns of relationships.

Indeed, past research has shown intrinsic and extrinsic binding abilities to be distinct in their neurophysiological signatures (Ecker et al., 2007; Zimmer & Ecker, 2010), relationships with age (Old & Naveh-Benjamin, 2008), and performance under cognitive load (Allen et al., 2006).

text.text: Intrinsic binding would be expected to not share substantial variance with extrinsic binding, but further research is needed to evidence the binding functions that are encompassed by process-general Binding.

This study investigated the shared and unique variance between item-to-location binding, item-to-item binding, relational integration, relation processing, and perceptual feature binding and how they relate to Gf.
We found significant overlap between binding functions, but only item-to-item and item-to-location binding were best modelled as one ability, binding memory.

Moreover, the shared variance between binding memory and the other binding functions was well-represented by a process-general ability, Binding, which seems to represent the ability to form and use bindings in a goal-directed manner.
Binding was statistically indistinguishable from Gf while each individual binding function (apart from perceptual feature binding) uniquely related to Gf in a latent network analysis.

Taken together, these results indicate that, more so than any specific binding function, the general ability to form and use bindings in a goal-directed manner explains nearly all of the variance in Gf.
